newsitem.title: USA: Summations due in Oklahoma City bombing case.
newsitem.headline: Summations due in Oklahoma City bombing case.

text.p: Prosecutors and defence attorneys had one last chance on Thursday to convince the jury in the Oklahoma City bombing case of Timothy McVeigh's guilt or innocence.
A massive truck bomb killed 168 people and wounded more than 500 in April of 1995, tearing off the front of the Murrah federal building.

Closing arguments were slated to begin in the morning, with jury deliberations to follow. The anonymous jury, which was expected to be sequestered, was likely to continue its deliberations through the weekend if necessary.
If convicted of federal murder and conspiray charges, McVeigh, 29, faced the death penalty.
With the testimony over, the waiting became the hardest part, said Marsha Kight, who lost her 23-year-old daughter, Frankie Merrell, in the April 19, 1995 bombing.

"It brings back a lot of memories of when I was waiting for news of my daughter -- feeling powerless, afraid and not knowing what to expect," Kight said Wednesday outside the Denver federal courthouse where the trial was being held.
Testimony began April 25 and moved much more quickly than almost anyone expected, largely due to the no-nonsense approach of U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch.
"They did not belabor their witnesses," said Denver trial attorney Scott Robinson, who has followed the case. "Both sides get credit for that."

"The prosecutors will attempt to explain the mosaic of circumstantial, forensic amd co-conspirator evidence accumulated against McVeigh," Robinson said. "The defence will expose the weaknesses in the government's case."

Prosecutors based a major portion of their case on the FBI's findings of explosives residue on McVeigh's clothing and the fact he was carrying earplugs. They also relied on the testimony of Michael Fortier, an Army buddy of McVeigh's, and his wife, Lori Fortier.

Michael Fortier testified that McVeigh told him about his rage against the federal government and his plans to target the Alfred P. Murrah building in Oklahoma City. Lori Fortier described how McVeigh told her his plans to build the bomb with barrels inside a truck. He used soup cans on her kitchen floor to illustrate how he would lay out the barrels, she said.

Prosecutors claimed McVeigh bombed the building in anger over the government's siege two years earlier at the Branch Davidian complex in Waco, Texas. The siege, where some 80 people died, became a rallying cry for the extremist right wing that felt the federal government violated the Branch Davidians' constitutional rights.

The defence, which ended its case on Wednesday, presented 25 witnesses over four days. McVeigh's attorneys focused on the credibility of Michael Fortier and FBI investigators who collected scientific evidence against their client.
They played wire-tapped telephone conversations to discredit Fortier, who can be heard telling friends he hoped to make "one cool mill" by selling his story to the media.
"I'll just give them something juicy," he said, adding he know nothing about McVeigh's alleged crimes.
Clearly hoping questions about the FBI's investigation could induce jurors to question its findings, the defence also targeted the standards and procedures at the agency's crime lab.
The lab was found contaminated with explosives residue just weeks after the bombing, one agent testified. But he said he had no proof any evidence was tainted.

The explosives residue was the prosecution's best scientific evidence against McVeigh, who was wearing the clothes when he was arrested soon after the blast by a state trooper who noticed his car was missing a license plate.

His attorneys also raised the spectre of John Doe No. 2, an unidentified suspect who was never found. They proposed that an unidentified leg -- found at the bomb site and never explained -- could have belonged to the bomber.
